records.name: Sucre
records.current_summary:
No Sucre-specific law, enforcement practice or incident finding for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources. The national reporting they carry frames what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country: an international English-language paper (April 2025) reported the killing of Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten and thrown into a ravine in Bello, Antioquia, whose death intensified national alarm over transfeminicide; and an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in Caquetá distributing 'social cleansing' flyers giving trans women a week to leave, with 41 trans women killed nationally in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Those reported departments are not Sucre. Nothing in the record marks Sucre as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture; the 2024 investigation describes displacement of trans women across departmental lines, and the absence of Sucre-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.

sources.claim: El País English edition (14 April 2025) reports Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon with no one arrested; the article states hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. That national transfemicide alarm is the picture this department is assessed against; the report contains no Sucre-specific information.

The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women, quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide (recording the killings as ordinary cases), and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. This national armed-group violence and displacement baseline is what this department is assessed against; the report contains no Sucre-specific information.

records.name: Córdoba
records.current_summary:
No department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Córdoba: the country research classified it among the units whose risk sits in the national and departmental homicide counts only, without a sub-national deviation material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed alongside the national position.

National context from the sources: the country's monitoring bodies recorded 270 LGBTIQ+ killings in 2025 (one every 32 hours, a 63% increase on 2024's 164), with violence expanding territorially into departments where the state response is weakest; no Colombian department criminalises anything about being trans, and gender-identity recognition is administered nationally. The articles cited for this unit document the national picture (the transfeminicide in Bello, Antioquia, and armed-group 'social cleansing' in Caquetá) and none reports findings specific to Córdoba.

sources.claim: EL PAÍS English (14 Apr 2025) reports the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia: she was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of a cardiac arrest that afternoon; police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally the article reports 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, and cites earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. It contains no Córdoba-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is national context: lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, filmed, with the perpetrator unarrested.

The Guardian (30 Jul 2024) documented armed groups in Caquetá department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. It reports eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. No Córdoba-specific finding appears; the territorial-violence-and-displacement pattern by armed actors is the claim this record relies on.

records.name: Guainía
records.current_summary: This department lies in the country's frontier 'orden publico' belt, where armed groups rather than departmental police effectively regulate conduct; regional reporting documents trans women displaced from frontier departments because of their gender identity, amid territorial expansion of anti-LGBTIQ violence nationally (one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025, 63% up on 2024). No department-specific legal or enforcement deviation beyond national homicide counts; risk assessed on the national framework.

The killings didn't stop there' - follow-up reporting on continuing LGBTQ+ killings after the Millerey case, with gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths (crawl captured mainly navigation; full text unavailable).

The Guardian investigation (30 Jul 2024) documents armed groups in Caqueta department: three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed, and after hiding for a week she fled at night; 'social cleansing' flyers appeared on Caqueta streets and via WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. It reports eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. It contains no Guainía-specific finding; the national armed-group violence, threats and displacement pattern is the claim this record relies on.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Colombia
sources.claim: National-framework page defining the legal regime a trans visitor to Guainía stands under: Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011, and the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016 (first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016), having granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights in three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 and full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration in November 2015. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X), and adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request; gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. The department adds no separate legal regime, so this page fixes the visitor's formal legal exposure against which the record's armed-group violence findings are weighed.

records.name: Arauca
records.current_summary:
Arauca's own local situation for trans visitors is not established in the audited record — the frontier "public order" characterisation attached to it previously appears in no cited source, and a widely quoted per-32-hours killing statistic belongs to other compilations, so neither is repeated here. What is sourced is national: the killing of a trans woman in Antioquia (April 2025) that prompted a presidential investigation order; 13 trans people killed nationally in Q1 2025 and 41 trans women in 2023; and armed groups circulating "social cleansing" threats in at least one department (Caquetá, 2024). Impunity for anti-LGBTQ killings is near-total nationally.

Treated honestly, that means a visitor to Arauca faces the national pattern — high lethality, very low conviction, episodic state response — with no department-specific aggravation or protection on the record.

records.name: Casanare
records.current_summary:
Casanare has no department-specific law, enforcement practice or incident concerning trans visitors in the audited record; the visitor's exposure is the national picture. That picture, as sourced, is a country where an August 2025 investigation continued reporting killings of queer and trans people after a viral torture-murder of a trans woman earlier that year, with gangs linked to queer and trans deaths, and where a 2024 report documented armed groups issuing "social cleansing" ultimatums to trans women in at least one department — 41 trans women killed nationally in 2023, 8 more between February and April 2024.

Against that baseline Casanare adds nothing on either side: no documented local aggravation, and no documented local protection.

records.name: Cauca
records.current_summary:
For Cauca the audited record carries no regional statute, enforcement practice or incident specific to trans visitors, so the national baseline stands: an August 2025 investigation documents continuing killings of queer and trans people — gangs linked to queer and trans deaths after a viral torture-murder of a trans woman that year — and a 2024 national report records armed groups in Cauca's larger region circulating "social cleansing" flyers giving trans women ultimatums to leave or be killed, amid 41 recorded killings of trans women in 2023.

Armed-group presence is strong in Cauca's countryside nationally, but no source on this record ties that to trans-specific local mechanisms; the file deliberately stops at the national pattern.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The article documents the national legal framework that a trans visitor stands under in the department of Cauca: consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Colombia since 1981; Congress passed a national ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in 2011; and in April 2016 the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage, with the country's first same-sex wedding taking place in Cali on 24 May 2016. It also records that legal gender change has been possible since 1993 and that birth certificates offer markers F, M, NB and T. No Cauca-specific statute or incident appears in the article, so the department is assessed at this national floor.

No department-specific legal deviation; risk assessed on the national framework.
